messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Aryan Desai grew up in a cramped Queens apartment where survival depended on anticipating his stepfather’s moods. When anger flared, his stepfather would drag Aryan to the hallway and press his bare back against the iron radiator, holding him there until his skin burned. He was routinely locked in the narrow bathroom at night, the heavy deadbolt sliding shut with a deafening clack that vibrated through the floorboards. Aryan learned to survive by shrinking inward, believing that stillness and silence were the only shields against violence. He carried that conditioning into his career as a police detective, but the sensory architecture of his childhood began to hijack his adult life. Now at thirty-six, the sudden slam of a precinct interview room door or a cold draft sweeping through the evidence bay would send his pulse spiking long before his conscious mind registered why. Each time one of those cues hit, a corrosive internal narrative took over. He had come to believe that his racing heart meant there was something fundamentally wrong with him as a person, a defective self that would never function normally. He felt like he didn't know himself anymore, watching his own reactions with detached horror. The way his body betrayed him convinced him that his reactions since the event showed he was a lousy coper, utterly unequipped to handle everyday stress. Because he was certain that his own nervous system was broken, Aryan began to construct a life designed to keep those sensory cues at bay. He avoided people, turning down dinners with Maya and leaving precinct calls unanswered, telling himself he just needed to process. He delayed sleep, pacing the apartment or scrolling through case files until two in the morning, because lying still made him acutely aware of sleeping alone in the dark. He avoided going out to any social events, crafting excuses about overtime, slowly isolating himself in a quiet that felt safer than the threat of surprise. The habits he built to protect himself quickly became proof of his worst fears. Each night he spent awake only deepened his conviction that he was a bad coper, unable to manage his own rest without spiraling. When he finally did collapse into bed, the isolation left him hyper-vigilant, and any unfamiliar temperature on his skin felt like an immediate warning. He was certain that his own avoidance was making him weaker, that by refusing to walk past a slamming door or sit in a temperature-controlled room, he was teaching his brain that danger was unavoidable. The less he engaged with the world, the more his senses tuned to threat, and the more his negative self-appraisals swelled. Those negative appraisals fed directly back into his sensory landscape, turning ordinary moments into crises. His belief that he was defective made him scan every environment for signs of failure, and that scanning kept his alertness dangerously high. When Maya left for work, the quiet apartment felt oppressive, and Aryan found himself fixated on the temperature of the air against his forearms, hunting for the ghost of that hallway radiator. What frightened him most was the realization that his own mind was manufacturing the threats he spent every day running from. The loop had tightened over the past nine months until his marriage was fraying and his caseload was slipping, with witnesses complaining about his jumpy demeanor during interviews. He came to the clinic last week because he could no longer pretend the exhaustion was just work stress, and because the thought of one night spent completely alone, waiting for a door to slam, made his hands shake. He hoped to find a way to trust his own body again, even if it meant learning that not every sudden noise was a prelude to violence.
